In the United Kingdom, the communications regulator requires the World Cup to be listed as a 'designated sporting event', meaning in theory all World Cup matches must be broadcast live on free-to-air television, with broadcasters BBC and ITV not inserting advertisements during the water break at half-time. China's National Radio and Television Administration, on the other hand, stipulates that broadcasting rights for the World Cup, Asian Games and Olympic Games must be owned exclusively by CCTV, which in recent years has obtained the rights for this tournament from FIFA at a low price on a temporary basis.

PCCW has won broadcasting rights for three consecutive tournaments; per-capita cost ranks among the highest in the world

Returning to Hong Kong, PCCW — which simultaneously holds free-to-air and pay-TV licences, as well as fixed-line and mobile telecommunications licences — has secured World Cup broadcasting rights for three consecutive editions. In contrast, Television Broadcasts (TVB) once recorded losses from broadcasting the World Cup, while Cable TV has already discontinued its pay-TV business, leaving no other bidder in the market with cross-platform and bundling advantages.

It is believed that FIFA has fully taken into account the pressure on PCCW to retain customers amid the 'cord-cutting' trend, and accordingly charged Hong Kong a certain fee for the broadcasting rights. The exclusive Hong Kong broadcasting rights for this World Cup are reported to have been concluded at approximately HK$170 million, slightly lower than before, yet on a per-capita basis Hong Kong still ranks among the highest globally. Commercial sponsorship shapes the rules of the game — far more than just 'watching football and incidentally spotting boots'

During the World Cup, from pitch-side advertising to the Video Assistant Referee (VAR), every spot is a golden opportunity to capture the audience's attention — commercial sponsorship and licensing naturally become another important revenue source for FIFA. FIFA divides its sponsors into four main tiers, while sponsors around the world also quietly compete for global influence every four years.

In recent editions, the top-tier FIFA Partners have consistently been globally renowned brands, including Adidas, Coca-Cola, Hyundai and Visa. Partners also include potential host nations — for instance, Qatar Airways has been a sponsor since 2017, while Saudi Aramco, the oil company of Saudi Arabia (host of the 2034 World Cup), is likewise sponsoring this tournament in a publicly disclosed deal with FIFA.

Chinese sponsors, which had attracted attention in recent years thanks to their Chinese-language advertising slogans, have seen the value of their sponsorship for this tournament drop by nearly 70 percent. The Wanda Group, which had served as a top-tier partner in the previous two editions, was replaced due to unpaid sponsorship fees and withdrew along with smartphone brand Vivo. The remaining major Chinese sponsors include Lenovo and Hisense, which respectively hold naming rights for the newly introduced 'Referee Camera' and the VAR display equipment, as well as Mengniu, which often appears with its baffling slogan suggesting trying soft milk instead of milk.

Haaland endorses Wong Lo Kat; Messi features in Mengniu ad

The time difference for this tournament and China-US relations may have affected the willingness of Chinese sponsors to participate, but Chinese-funded enterprises may have realised that the promotional effect of celebrity endorsements could outweigh brand exposure. The heated online discussion over the advertisement starring Norwegian striker Erling Haaland for Wong Lo Kat herbal tea is a clear case in point. French star Kylian Mbappé endorses 'Be Water', the electrolyte drink under Dongpeng Beverage, which has been prominently displayed in Hong Kong this year, with the ad even deliberately scheduled to air during the water break. The changing composition of World Cup sponsors is likewise reshaping the tournament's landscape. Although American domestic brands such as Bank of America, telecom carrier Verizon, and Frito-Lay, owner of Lay's crisps, have successively joined, sponsorships from companies of the host nation tend to be short-lived. As for Japanese electronics companies, once a familiar presence in World Cup sponsorship, their visibility on the pitch has been waning — something some speculate is a sign of Japan's economic decline, when in fact many enterprises have shifted towards the more profitable commercial market rather than consumer electronics, lacking the incentive to pursue global exposure.

All non-sponsor brands prohibited inside the venues

The once-impressive collective presence of Chinese sponsors along the pitch-side at recent World Cups may not in future be replaced by another emerging country, but rather increasingly by ambush marketing lurking outside the stadiums. Citing the protection of sponsors' rights, FIFA rigorously enforces 'clean stadium' measures, prohibiting the appearance of any non-sponsor brands inside the venues.
